deck.title: Passage of Information from Parents to Offspring

front_blocks.md: Define **haploid (n)**.

back_blocks.md: A **haploid** cell contains a **single set** of chromosomes — one of each type, with **no homologous pairs**.
Gametes are haploid.

front_blocks.md: Define **diploid (2n)**.

back_blocks.md: A **diploid** cell contains **two complete sets** of chromosomes (2n) — one set inherited from each parent, arranged in **homologous pairs**.

front_blocks.md: In humans, what are the **diploid** and **haploid** chromosome numbers?

back_blocks.md: **Diploid (2n) = 46** — 23 homologous pairs in body cells.
**Haploid (n) = 23** — found in gametes.

cards.front_md: In humans, what are the **diploid** and **haploid** chromosome numbers?

front_blocks.md: Why is a **reduction division** needed during meiosis in the production of gametes?

back_blocks.md: Meiosis **halves** the chromosome number from **diploid (2n)** to **haploid (n)**.
This means that when two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the **diploid number is restored** in the zygote.

front_blocks.md: What would happen to the chromosome number over generations if gametes were **diploid**?

back_blocks.md: The chromosome number would **double every generation**.
The reduction division in meiosis prevents this by keeping gametes haploid.

A haploid cell contains homologous pairs of chromosomes.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

front_blocks.md: What is a **homologous pair** of chromosomes?

back_blocks.md: A pair of chromosomes — **one maternal and one paternal** — that:
- carry the **same genes** at the **same loci**
- are the **same length** with the centromere in the **same position**
The alleles they carry may differ.

front_blocks.md: Do **homologous chromosomes** carry identical alleles?

back_blocks.md: They carry the **same genes** at the **same loci**, but the **alleles** of those genes may be **different**.

cards.front_md: Do **homologous chromosomes** carry identical alleles?

front_blocks.md: When and where do **homologous chromosomes** pair up?

back_blocks.md: During **prophase I of meiosis**.
Each homologous pair comes together to form a **bivalent**.

front_blocks.md: What are the **two divisions** of meiosis, and what separates in each?

back_blocks.md: **Meiosis I** (reduction division): **homologous chromosomes** are separated.
**Meiosis II**: **sister chromatids** are separated.
The result is **four haploid** cells.

cards.front_md: What are the **two divisions** of meiosis, and what separates in each?
cards.back_md:
**Meiosis I** (reduction division): **homologous chromosomes** are separated.

**Meiosis II**: **sister chromatids** are separated.

The result is **four haploid** cells.

front_blocks.md: Name the **main stages of meiosis** in order.

back_blocks.md: **Meiosis I:** prophase I → metaphase I → anaphase I → telophase I
**Meiosis II:** prophase II → metaphase II → anaphase II → telophase II

front_blocks.md: What happens during **prophase I** of meiosis?

back_blocks.md: - Chromosomes **condense** and become visible
- The **nuclear envelope** breaks down
- **Homologous chromosomes pair up** to form bivalents
- **Crossing over** occurs
- The **spindle** begins to form

front_blocks.md: What happens during **metaphase I** and **anaphase I**?

back_blocks.md: **Metaphase I:** bivalents line up at the equator, attached to spindle fibres, with **random orientation**.
**Anaphase I:** **homologous chromosomes** are pulled to opposite poles (sister chromatids stay joined).

cards.front_md: What happens during **metaphase I** and **anaphase I**?
cards.back_md:

front_blocks.md: What is separated during **anaphase II**, and how does this differ from anaphase I?

back_blocks.md: **Anaphase II:** **sister chromatids** are separated to opposite poles.
**Anaphase I:** whole **homologous chromosomes** are separated.

cards.front_md: What is separated during **anaphase II**, and how does this differ from anaphase I?
cards.back_md:
**Anaphase II:** **sister chromatids** are separated to opposite poles.

**Anaphase I:** whole **homologous chromosomes** are separated.

front_blocks.md: How does **cytokinesis** at the end of meiosis differ between animal and plant cells?

back_blocks.md: **Animal cells:** the **cell surface membrane** pinches inwards (cleavage furrow) to divide the cell.
**Plant cells:** a **cell plate** forms and a new cell wall is laid down.

front_blocks.md: How do you tell **anaphase I** from **anaphase II** in a photomicrograph?

back_blocks.md: **Anaphase I:** whole chromosomes (each still **two chromatids**) move to the poles.

front_blocks.md: How can you distinguish **metaphase I of meiosis** from **metaphase of mitosis**?

back_blocks.md: In **meiosis I**, chromosomes line up as **homologous pairs (bivalents)** at the equator.
In **mitosis**, chromosomes line up **singly**.

front_blocks.md: Define **crossing over**.

back_blocks.md: During **prophase I**, homologous chromosomes exchange sections of **chromatid**, swapping **alleles** between them.
This produces **new combinations** of alleles.

front_blocks.md: What is **random orientation** (independent assortment) in meiosis?

back_blocks.md: In **metaphase I**, each homologous pair lines up at the equator **independently** of the others.
So maternal and paternal chromosomes are distributed to gametes in **random combinations**.

cards.front_md: What is **random orientation** (independent assortment) in meiosis?
cards.back_md:

So maternal and paternal chromosomes are distributed to gametes in **random combinations**.

front_blocks.md: How does **crossing over** produce genetic variation?

back_blocks.md: It swaps alleles between homologous chromosomes, creating **new allele combinations** on each chromosome and therefore **genetically different gametes**.

cards.front_md: How does **crossing over** produce genetic variation?

front_blocks.md: How does **random orientation** of chromosomes produce variation?

back_blocks.md: Homologous pairs (and sister chromatids in meiosis II) can line up in **many different combinations**.
This mixes maternal and paternal chromosomes, giving a huge variety of possible **gametes**.

cards.front_md: How does **random orientation** of chromosomes produce variation?
cards.back_md:
Homologous pairs (and sister chromatids in meiosis II) can line up in **many different combinations**.

This mixes maternal and paternal chromosomes, giving a huge variety of possible **gametes**.

front_blocks.md: How does the **random fusion of gametes** at fertilisation produce variation?

back_blocks.md: Any male gamete can fuse with any female gamete.
Because the gametes are already genetically different, this random fusion produces **genetically different individuals**.
